title: The robot hand that never loses at rock paper scissors
hook: A robot hand wins rock paper scissors every time by being too fast to see.
peek: In 2012 a lab at the University of Tokyo showed a robot hand that wins rock paper scissors every single game. It does not read minds. A high-speed camera watches your hand form its shape, and the robot answers before you notice.
lede: Rock paper scissors, called janken in Japan, is meant to be a game of pure chance. In 2012, the Ishikawa Watanabe Laboratory at the University of Tokyo showed off a robot hand that never loses. It does not predict anything. It simply watches the human hand start to form rock, paper or scissors, and plays the winning shape almost instantly.

bullets.text: The robot's camera takes about 1,000 pictures every second, so it captures a new frame roughly every millisecond. Software reads the shape of the human hand from those frames as the fingers begin to move.

The hand itself was built in the lab for fast, nimble tasks, and it can change shape in a tiny fraction of a second. Its answer arrives so quickly that to a human the two hands seem to move at the same moment.
Strictly speaking, the robot cheats: it moves a moment after you. The trick works because human eyes and reactions are far too slow to notice that tiny delay, so the win looks fair.
The janken robot was a showcase for the lab's research into high-speed vision and fast machines, the kind of work that can help robots catch, sort and handle things quickly.
